title: Early humans and the first civilizations
note: Farming began about 12,000 years ago and let people settle in one place. In fertile river valleys (the Tigris and Euphrates, the Nile, the Indus and the Yellow River) surplus food supported cities, rulers, priests, writing and trade: the marks of civilization.

read.title: From villages to cities
text: For most of the human past, people lived in small bands that hunted animals and gathered wild plants. About 12,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent of southwest Asia, some groups began planting wheat and barley and keeping sheep and goats. Farming spread and also began on its own in other regions, including China, Mexico and New Guinea. Historians call this change the Neolithic Revolution.

Farming produced more food than hunting, and a surplus changed everything. Villages grew into towns. Not everyone had to farm, so some people became potters, metalworkers, priests, soldiers and scribes. Leaders organized labor to dig canals and build walls and temples.

The first cities rose in river valleys where floods left rich soil. In Sumer, between the Tigris and Euphrates, city-states such as Uruk and Ur built ziggurats and kept records in cuneiform. Along the Nile, Egypt became one kingdom ruled by a pharaoh and built the pyramids. In the Indus valley, planned cities like Mohenjo-Daro had grid streets and drains. On the Yellow River, the Shang kings wrote questions to their ancestors on oracle bones. Writing, cities, specialized work and organized government are the features historians use to define a civilization.
